chapters.reflection: The book opens with three questions, each answered by itself. Learning is a pleasure when it is practised over time, friends who come from far away are a joy, and the last line turns inward: the measure of a person is how they bear being overlooked. The order runs from the self, to company, to the world's indifference.
chapters.question: Which of the three is hardest for you today: to keep at something, to welcome someone, or to go unnoticed without resentment?

chapters.reflection: Master Yu, one of the disciples, argues that people who are good to their parents and elder brothers rarely stir up trouble. His image is of a tree: attend to the root, and the branches follow. The household comes first in this order of things, and the larger virtue grows out of it.
chapters.question: What in your own life works as a root, so that other things grow from it without effort?

chapters.reflection: One sentence, and it returns more than once in the book. Smooth talk and an ingratiating face are rarely found together with real goodness. It does not say they never are; it says they seldom are, and asks us to notice the pattern.
chapters.question: When were you last persuaded more by how something was said than by what was said?

chapters.reflection: Master Zeng examines himself each day on three points: whether he was faithful in working for others, sincere with friends, and whether he practised what he was taught. The questions are about conduct, not feelings, and each one names a relation: the people he serves, his friends, his teacher.
chapters.question: If you asked yourself three questions every evening, what would they be?
chapters.exercise: Tonight, before sleep, ask Zeng's three questions of the day just past, and answer each in a single honest sentence.

chapters.reflection: Government here is a short list: attention to affairs, good faith, thrift, care for people, and calling on the people's labour only in the right season, when the fields can spare them. A thousand chariots meant a middling state. The advice is practical before it is lofty.
chapters.question: Which item on this list would matter most in a place you know, a workplace or a town?

chapters.reflection: A young person's duties are named in order: be good at home, respectful outside, careful and truthful, kind to all and close to the good. Only when there is strength to spare should they turn to letters. Conduct is the first lesson and books the second.
chapters.question: Do you think conduct can be learned before reading, or only through it?

chapters.reflection: Zixia describes someone who prefers worth to beauty, gives their full strength to their parents and their life to their lord, and keeps faith with friends. Even if people say this person never studied, Zixia insists they have. Learning is judged by what it produces.
chapters.question: Whom do you know who never studied in the usual sense and yet has learned, in Zixia's sense?

chapters.reflection: Four short rules: be serious, or learning will not hold; put good faith first; do not befriend those who are not your equals; when you have faults, do not be afraid to correct them. The third rule is often read as "befriend those who can help you grow". The last is the one the book returns to.
chapters.question: What fault have you been slow to correct, and what makes correcting it frightening?

chapters.reflection: Master Zeng ties public virtue to how carefully the dead are mourned and the long departed remembered in sacrifice. Care for those who can no longer repay it is, for him, what makes a people's character deep. The rites are a form of memory.
chapters.question: How do the people around you remember those who came before them?

chapters.reflection: Ziqin wonders whether Confucius asks for news of each government or is simply told. Zigong answers that the Master is gentle, upright, courteous, frugal and deferential, and so people tell him. His way of asking is not to ask in the usual way at all.
chapters.question: Have you found that people tell you more when you press, or when you are the kind of person they want to tell?

chapters.reflection: While a father lives, look at the son's intentions; after his death, look at his conduct. If for three years he keeps to his father's way, he may be called filial. The three years match the length of mourning. The chapter returns almost word for word as IV.20.
chapters.question: What would it mean to keep someone's way for a time after they are gone, and when should the keeping end?

chapters.reflection: Master Yu says that in ritual, harmony and ease are what matter most, and the old kings prized them in great and small things alike. Yet ease that is not held by ritual will not do either. Form without ease is stiff; ease without form drifts.
chapters.question: Where in your day is there a form you keep that also lets you be at ease?

chapters.reflection: When a promise is close to what is right, it can be kept. When respect is close to what is proper, it keeps shame away. When you rely on people who will not let you down, they can be relied on to the end. Each clause is about choosing well at the beginning.
chapters.question: Is there a promise you made that you could keep only because it was right to begin with?

chapters.reflection: Confucius describes someone who does not seek a full stomach or a comfortable house, is quick in action and careful in speech, and goes to those who have the Way to be set straight. Such a person, he says, loves learning. Learning is again a matter of a whole life, not of books alone.
chapters.question: Who would you go to, today, to be set straight?

chapters.reflection: Zigong is pleased with being poor without flattery and rich without pride. Confucius answers that it is better still to be poor and joyful, rich and fond of ritual. Zigong recognises a line from the Odes about cutting and polishing jade: good is not the end, it can be worked further. The Master is delighted that he made the leap himself.
chapters.question: What in you is good enough already, and could still be polished?

chapters.reflection: The first book ends where it began, with being unknown. Confucius is not troubled that others do not know him; he is troubled that he does not know them. The worry is turned around and given a task.
chapters.question: Whom have you failed to understand, while worrying that you were not understood?

chapters.reflection: A ruler who governs by virtue is like the pole star: it stays in its place and the other stars turn around it. The image is of influence without force. The ruler does not chase anything; others orient themselves by him.
chapters.question: Is there someone whose steadiness, more than anything they said, set the direction for people around them?

chapters.reflection: Confucius sums up the three hundred poems of the Book of Odes in one phrase from one of them: no depraved thoughts, or thoughts that do not swerve. Whatever the poems are about, love, war, complaint, they are honest. The summary is about the spirit of the collection, not its subject matter.
chapters.question: What book, song or poem would you sum up in a single line, and which line?

chapters.reflection: Lead people by laws and keep them in line with punishments, and they will try to escape the punishment and feel no shame. Lead them by virtue and ritual, and they will have a sense of shame and set themselves right. The chapter is the book's clearest statement of how it thinks order is made.
chapters.question: In your own experience, has a rule or the example of a person done more to change how you behave?

chapters.reflection: The Master's life in six stages: at fifteen set on learning, at thirty standing firm, at forty without doubts, at fifty knowing the decrees of Heaven, at sixty with an ear attuned, at seventy following his heart without overstepping. It is the only autobiography the book gives him, and it describes a long ripening rather than a single conversion.
chapters.question: If you had to name the stage you are in now, what would you call it?
chapters.exercise: Write one line for each decade of your life so far, saying what you were set on then.

chapters.reflection: Meng Yi asks about filial piety and is told "not disobeying". Later, in the carriage, Confucius explains to Fan Chi what he meant: serve parents by ritual while they live, bury them by ritual, sacrifice to them by ritual. Meng Yi belonged to one of the great families that used rites above their station, so "not disobeying" may have meant not disobeying ritual itself.
chapters.question: Have you ever given a short answer that only made sense once you explained it to someone else?

chapters.reflection: Asked about filial piety by Meng Wu, Confucius answers with a sentence about parents: they worry that their children will fall ill. The line can be read two ways: give them nothing else to worry about, or know that this worry is how they love you. The chapter leaves both open.
chapters.question: Which reading of this chapter seems truer to you, and why?

chapters.reflection: To Ziyou, Confucius says that filial piety nowadays means supporting one's parents, but even dogs and horses are fed. Without reverence, what makes the difference? The point is not the provision but the attitude in which it is given.
chapters.question: What is the difference, for you, between looking after someone and respecting them?

chapters.reflection: To Zixia, the answer is that the hard part is one's countenance. Doing the work for elders and serving them food and wine first is not yet the thing itself. The expression with which it is done tells more than the doing.
chapters.question: Does your face, when you help someone, say the same as your hands?

chapters.reflection: Yan Hui listens all day without objecting, and Confucius wonders whether he is slow. Then he watches how Hui lives on his own and finds that he carries out everything he heard. Silence in a student, the chapter suggests, is not always absence of thought.
chapters.question: Whom have you misjudged as dull because they did not argue?

chapters.reflection: Three ways to know a person: look at what they do, observe how they do it and why, and see where they find their rest. Then, twice, how can a person hide? The repetition sounds like a teacher who has watched people for many years.
chapters.question: Where do you find your rest, and what would it tell an observer about you?

chapters.reflection: Keep warming up what you already know and come to know what is new, and you can be a teacher. The verb in the Chinese suggests reheating. Old knowledge is not a store to be kept but something to be brought back to warmth again and again.
chapters.question: What old piece of knowledge have you not revisited in years?

chapters.reflection: The junzi, Legge's "accomplished scholar" here, is not a vessel, not a tool made for a single use. A person of worth is not defined by one function. This six-word chapter is often quoted against narrow specialisation, though its first sense is about character, not careers.
chapters.question: Is there a part of you that has been made into a single-purpose tool?

chapters.reflection: Zigong, who was a gifted talker, asks about the junzi. He is told: such a person acts first and then speaks in accordance with the action. The answer is fitted to the asker.
chapters.question: What have you said you would do that you have not yet done?

chapters.reflection: The junzi is broad in sympathy and does not form cliques; the small man forms cliques and is not broad. Legge's "catholic" means universal, the nineteenth-century sense of the word. The contrast between the junzi and the small man runs through the whole book.
chapters.question: Where do you find yourself taking a side before you have considered the matter?

chapters.reflection: Learning without thought is lost labour; thinking without learning is dangerous. Each needs the other. The chapter refuses both the student who memorises and the thinker who never reads.
chapters.question: Which of the two do you lean toward, learning or thinking?

chapters.reflection: Legge reads this as a warning against studying heterodox doctrines. Other translators read the same words as "attacking the other end" or "working on the wrong end", which would make it a warning about method rather than about rival schools. The short chapter has been argued over for two thousand years.
chapters.question: How do you decide which ideas are worth your attention, and which only distract?

chapters.reflection: To Zilu, the confident one, Confucius explains: when you know something, hold that you know it; when you do not, admit that you do not. That is knowledge. It is the most quoted definition in the book, and it is also a gentle correction of the person it was addressed to.
chapters.question: What do you claim to know that you would have to admit you do not?
chapters.exercise: Once today, when asked something you are unsure of, say plainly that you do not know.

chapters.reflection: Zizhang is studying with an eye on an official salary. Confucius does not scold him; he tells him how: hear much, leave aside what is doubtful, speak carefully of the rest; see much, leave aside what is risky, act carefully on the rest. With few mistakes in speech and few regrets in conduct, a salary follows.
chapters.question: What would you set aside as doubtful before you speak today?

chapters.reflection: Duke Ai of Lu asks how to win the people's obedience. Raise the upright and set them over the crooked, and the people will follow; do the reverse, and they will not. The answer is about whom a ruler promotes, which the people can see.
chapters.question: In a group you belong to, who gets raised, and what does that teach everyone else?

chapters.reflection: Ji Kangzi, the most powerful man in Lu, asks how to make the people respectful, loyal and eager. Each answer turns the question back to him: be dignified and they will respect you; be filial and kind and they will be loyal; promote the good and teach the unable and they will be eager. The ruler is asked to change himself.
chapters.question: What do you ask of others that you have not first asked of yourself?

chapters.reflection: Someone asks why Confucius does not take part in government. He quotes the Book of Documents on being filial and brotherly, and says that this too is government. Ordering a household is part of ordering the world. The answer also explains, without complaint, why he is out of office.
chapters.question: What counts as public work that is usually not counted?

chapters.reflection: A person without good faith is like a cart without the pin that joins the yoke to the shaft: it cannot move. The image is a small, essential piece of wood. Trust is not decoration; without it nothing goes anywhere.
chapters.question: What small promise, broken, would stop something larger from moving?

chapters.reflection: Zizhang asks whether the future can be known. Confucius answers from history: the Yin took over the rites of the Xia, the Zhou those of the Yin, and what each added and removed can be known. So even a hundred generations on can be known. He reads the future as continuity in ritual, not as prediction.
chapters.question: What in your own life has been carried forward from your parents' time, and what has been changed?

chapters.reflection: Two sentences put side by side. Sacrificing to spirits that are not one's own is flattery. Seeing what is right and not doing it is a lack of courage. One is doing what one should not, the other not doing what one should.
chapters.question: What have you seen to be right recently and not done?

chapters.reflection: The head of the Ji family had eight rows of dancers perform in his courtyard, a display reserved for the Son of Heaven. Confucius says: if he can bear to do this, what can he not bear to do? Book III opens with ritual as a matter of station, and with a family that has taken more than its place.
chapters.question: What small overreach, in someone you know or in yourself, told you something larger?

chapters.reflection: The three great families of Lu closed their sacrifices with a hymn written for the royal house, which speaks of princes assisting and the Son of Heaven solemn. Confucius asks what those words can mean in their halls. A text sung in the wrong place becomes a kind of lie.
chapters.question: Have you used words, at some occasion, that did not belong to it?

chapters.reflection: If a person is not humane, what is ritual to them? If a person is not humane, what is music to them? Legge renders ren here as "the virtues proper to humanity". Form depends on the heart that fills it.
chapters.question: Which of your habits of courtesy are still filled with feeling, and which have gone empty?

chapters.reflection: Lin Fang asks what is fundamental in ceremonies. A great question, says the Master: in festivity, better frugal than lavish; in mourning, better deep grief than perfect detail. When in doubt, choose the inner over the outward.
chapters.question: At the last ceremony you attended, a wedding or a funeral, what mattered most?

chapters.reflection: Legge reads this as: the tribes of the east and north have their rulers, unlike the Chinese states, which are without them, a lament for the disorder of Confucius's own land. Other readers take it the opposite way, that the tribes even with rulers are not equal to the states without them. Both readings say something about how Zhou China saw its neighbours.
chapters.question: When you compare your own place with another, which way does the comparison usually run?

chapters.reflection: The Ji family head prepares to sacrifice to Mount Tai, a rite for the ruler of the state alone. Confucius asks Ran You, who served the family, whether he can stop it, and Ran You says he cannot. Will the mountain, Confucius asks, be less discerning than Lin Fang, who asked about the root of ritual?
chapters.question: When have you served someone and been unable to stop them doing wrong?

chapters.reflection: The junzi does not compete, except perhaps in archery, and even there he bows to his opponent before and after, and drinks the forfeit with him. Legge keeps the Chinese word here: "Chun-tsze". The point is that rivalry can be held inside a form that respects the other side.
chapters.question: Where do you compete, and what form keeps the competition decent?

chapters.reflection: Zixia asks about a line of an ode on a lovely smile and bright eyes on a plain ground. Confucius explains that colour is laid on after the white. Zixia leaps: so ritual comes after? The Master is pleased: now he can discuss the Odes with Shang, Zixia's personal name. Ritual is the colour; something plainer must come first.
chapters.question: What is the plain ground under your own good manners?

chapters.reflection: Confucius could describe the rites of the Xia and the Yin, he says, but the states descended from them, Qi and Song, do not keep enough documents or learned men to confirm him. If they did, he could prove what he says. He knows the difference between what he thinks and what he can show.
chapters.question: What do you believe that you could not prove?

chapters.reflection: At the great sacrifice, once the libation has been poured, Confucius has no wish to watch any more. He does not say why. Most commentators think the rest of the rite was performed carelessly, or by a family with no right to it.
chapters.question: When have you stayed to watch something you no longer believed in?

chapters.reflection: Asked to explain the great sacrifice, Confucius says he does not know; whoever did would find governing the world as easy as looking at this, and he points to his palm. It is a refusal and a claim at once: the meaning of ritual, truly grasped, would be enough to order everything.
chapters.question: Is there a question you answer with "I do not know" because the true answer is too large?

chapters.reflection: He sacrificed to the dead as if they were present, and to the spirits as if they were present. If he could not take part himself, it was as though he had not sacrificed. The chapter describes an attitude rather than a belief: being fully there.
chapters.question: What do you do half-present that would change if you were there entirely?
chapters.exercise: Choose one ordinary task today and do it as if the person it is for were in the room.

chapters.reflection: Wangsun Jia, a powerful minister of Wei, quotes a proverb: better to court the god of the stove than the god of the south-west corner. It is a hint that Confucius should court the minister rather than the ruler. Confucius answers that whoever offends Heaven has no one left to pray to.
chapters.question: When were you advised to flatter the useful person rather than the right one?

chapters.reflection: The Zhou dynasty could look back on the two before it, and its culture is rich and elegant for that reason. Confucius follows Zhou. He chooses a tradition that had itself learned from earlier ones.
chapters.question: Which tradition do you follow, and what did it inherit before you received it?

chapters.reflection: In the Grand Temple, Confucius asks about every detail, and someone sneers that the son of the man from Zou cannot know ritual. Hearing this, Confucius says: this is ritual. Asking, in a place where one is a guest, is itself correct conduct.
chapters.question: Where do you avoid asking for fear of looking ignorant?

chapters.reflection: In ceremonial archery, piercing the target's leather is not the point, because people's strength differs. That was the old way. The contest measured form and accuracy, not force.
chapters.question: What do you measure yourself by that is really only a measure of strength?

chapters.reflection: The sacrifice that announced the new moon had lapsed, but a sheep was still offered, and Zigong wanted to drop it. Confucius: you love the sheep, I love the ritual. As long as the sheep is offered, something of the rite survives to be restored.
chapters.question: What small remnant of a lapsed practice are you tempted to drop?

chapters.reflection: Serving one's ruler with full ritual is taken by others as flattery. In a court where the families ignored the forms, simply keeping them looked like fawning. Doing the correct thing can look like the wrong one from outside.
chapters.question: Have you been misread for doing something properly?

chapters.reflection: Duke Ding asks how a ruler should employ ministers and how ministers should serve. A ruler employs ministers by ritual; ministers serve the ruler with faithfulness, zhong. The relation runs both ways, and each side owes the other something.
chapters.question: In a relation where one person holds more power, what does the stronger one owe?

chapters.reflection: The first poem of the Odes, the Guanju, has joy without wantonness and sorrow without injury. Confucius praises it for measure in feeling, not for the absence of feeling.
chapters.question: When did a strong feeling of yours stay within measure?

chapters.reflection: Asked about the trees planted at the altars of the land, Zai Wo adds that the Zhou chose the chestnut to make the people tremble, a pun in Chinese. Confucius, hearing it, says: what is done need not be discussed, what is finished need not be argued, what is past need not be blamed. It reads as a rebuke that refuses to dwell.
chapters.question: What past mistake, yours or another's, would be better left without further blame?

chapters.reflection: Confucius calls Guan Zhong, the famous minister of Qi, small in capacity. Was he frugal? No, he had three residences and staff who did one job each. Did he know ritual? He set up a gate screen and a cup stand as only rulers did. If he knew ritual, who does not? In XIV the same man is praised for what he achieved.
chapters.question: Can you think of someone who did great good and was small in their habits?

chapters.reflection: Speaking to the music master of Lu, Confucius describes a piece: it begins with all parts together, then each is distinct yet in harmony, clear and flowing, until it ends. The description is a quiet model of how a group can work as well.
chapters.question: Where have you seen many people stay distinct and still move together?

chapters.reflection: A border warden asks to meet Confucius and comes out consoling the disciples: why grieve over his loss of office? The world has long lacked the Way, and Heaven will use your master as a wooden-tongued bell, the kind officials rang to call the people to hear a proclamation. An outsider sees a vocation in the failure.
chapters.question: Has a setback of yours ever turned out to be a calling?

chapters.reflection: The Shao, the music of the sage king Shun, was perfectly beautiful and perfectly good. The Wu, music of King Wu who took the throne by conquest, was perfectly beautiful but not perfectly good. Beauty and goodness are judged separately, and a work can have one without the other.
chapters.question: What have you admired as beautiful that you could not call good?

chapters.reflection: Holding high office without generosity, performing ritual without reverence, mourning without grief: how could Confucius look on such things? The book of ritual ends by naming three forms emptied of their content.
chapters.question: Which of these three have you seen, and which have you done?

chapters.reflection: It is humaneness that makes a neighbourhood beautiful. Someone who chooses a place to live without regard to it can hardly be called wise. Book IV, the book of ren, opens with the company one keeps as a place.
chapters.question: What makes the place you live good or poor, apart from its buildings?

chapters.reflection: Without ren a person cannot bear hardship long, nor enjoy good times long either. The humane rest in it; the wise find it profitable. Two kinds of goodness are distinguished: one that is at home in itself and one that sees its advantage.
chapters.question: Is your goodness more often at rest, or more often calculating its benefit?

chapters.reflection: Only the humane person can truly love others and truly dislike them. The claim is not that the good love everyone; it is that their likes and dislikes are not bent by self-interest, so they can be trusted.
chapters.question: Whose approval would you trust because you know it is not bent by their interest?

chapters.reflection: If the will is truly set on humaneness, there will be no wickedness. The chapter places the decisive moment in the direction of the will, before any action.
chapters.question: What is your will set on, today, before anything else?

chapters.reflection: Wealth and rank are what everyone wants, but not if they come the wrong way; poverty and low station are what everyone dislikes, but not to be escaped the wrong way. The junzi does not leave ren even for the length of a meal, in haste or in danger. Goodness is not a mood but a place one does not leave.
chapters.question: In what kind of haste do you most easily leave your own standards?

chapters.reflection: Confucius says he has never seen anyone who truly loved ren or truly hated what is not ren. Yet who has ever applied their strength to it for one day and found the strength lacking? He has not seen it. The demand is high and the door is open at the same time.
chapters.question: What would one whole day of trying look like for you?
chapters.exercise: Pick one hour today and give it fully to treating others well, then notice whether your strength ran out.

chapters.reflection: A person's faults are of a piece with the kind of person they are. Look at the faults and you will know the goodness. A generous person errs by giving too much, a careful one by holding back; the fault shows the character it comes from.
chapters.question: What does your most frequent fault say about what you value?

chapters.reflection: To hear the Way in the morning and die in the evening would be enough. It is the most quoted line of the book about how much the Way is worth. It does not say what the Way is; it says what it would be worth to know it.
chapters.question: What would you be content to have understood, if you understood nothing else?

chapters.reflection: A scholar who is set on the Way but ashamed of shabby clothes and plain food is not worth talking with. The chapter catches a contradiction: someone who claims a higher aim and is still measuring themselves by appearance.
chapters.question: Where are you still measuring yourself by appearance, while saying you care about something else?

chapters.reflection: In the world the junzi has nothing he must do and nothing he must refuse; he goes with what is right, yi. The chapter rejects both rigid rules and drifting. The measure is not a list of positions but rightness in the case.
chapters.question: What position do you hold out of habit rather than because it is right here?

chapters.reflection: The junzi thinks of virtue, the small man of land and comfort; the junzi thinks of the law, the small man of favours. What a person thinks about, the chapter says, shows which of the two they are.
chapters.question: What did you think about most today?

chapters.reflection: One who acts always with an eye to profit will be much resented. Twelve words in Legge, and the observation is social more than moral: people notice, and they keep count.
chapters.question: When did you resent someone for always looking to their own advantage, and did they know?

chapters.reflection: If a state can be governed by ritual and deference, what difficulty is there? If not, what use is ritual? Legge's "complaisance" is the Chinese rang, yielding, giving way to others. Ritual that does not include yielding is not really ritual.
chapters.question: Where would a little giving way make something easier?

chapters.reflection: Do not worry about having no position; worry about being fit for one. Do not worry about being unknown; seek to be worth knowing. The book turns the same worry around for the second time.
chapters.question: If no one noticed your work for a year, would you still do it the same way?

chapters.reflection: Confucius tells Zeng Shen that his Way has one thread running through it, and leaves. The other disciples ask what he meant, and Zeng says: zhong and shu, doing one's utmost and measuring others by oneself, nothing more. Legge renders the pair as "true to the principles of our nature and the benevolent exercise of them to others". Whether Zeng's summary is the Master's is something the chapter leaves to the reader.
chapters.question: If your own life has one thread, what would you name it?

chapters.reflection: The junzi understands what is right; the small man understands what pays. The line is about what each person is fluent in, what their mind turns to without effort.
chapters.question: Which language are you more fluent in, what is right or what pays?

chapters.reflection: When you see someone worthy, think of becoming their equal; when you see someone unworthy, look inward and examine yourself. Both encounters are turned into work on oneself. Neither ends in envy or contempt.
chapters.question: Whom did you meet recently who could serve as either kind of mirror?
chapters.exercise: The next time someone irritates you today, ask whether you share the fault, before you judge it.

chapters.reflection: In serving parents, a child may object, but gently. If they will not listen, the child keeps respectful and does not give up, and does not complain even when it is hard. This is a description of conduct in the society of the time, where the child's place was below the parent's; the chapter asks for persistence and respect together, not for silence.
chapters.question: How do you disagree with someone you also respect?

chapters.reflection: While parents are alive, a son does not travel far, and if he does travel, he must have a fixed destination. In a world without letters that arrived quickly, a parent's worry needed somewhere to rest. It is advice from a time of slow roads.
chapters.question: Who would worry if they did not know where you were, and do they know?

chapters.reflection: The second half of I.11 returns almost word for word: if for three years a son does not change his father's way, he may be called filial. The repetition is one sign that the book was gathered from several sources rather than composed in one sitting.
chapters.question: What do you think the compilers meant by keeping a repeated saying twice?

chapters.reflection: One must know the ages of one's parents, with joy that they have reached them and with fear that they are growing old. Two feelings for one fact. The chapter asks for attention more than for any action.
chapters.question: How old are the people you love most, and what do you feel when you count the years?

chapters.reflection: The ancients were slow to speak because they were ashamed when their actions did not keep up with their words. Shame here is not humiliation but a sense of proportion between saying and doing.
chapters.question: What have you announced that your actions have not yet caught up with?

chapters.reflection: Those who hold themselves in check seldom go wrong. Legge's "the cautious seldom err" is the shortest saying in the book. It praises restraint, not timidity.
chapters.question: Where would a moment's restraint have spared you trouble this week?

chapters.reflection: The junzi wishes to be hesitant in speech and quick in action. The same thought appears in II.13 and IV.22, in different words. It is one of the book's steadiest themes.
chapters.question: Would the people who know you describe you as slow to speak or quick to speak?

chapters.reflection: Virtue, de, is never alone; it will have neighbours. Goodness attracts its own company, sooner or later. The chapter is a comfort for anyone who feels isolated in trying.
chapters.question: Who has been a neighbour to your better self?

chapters.reflection: Ziyou observes that frequent remonstrance with a ruler leads to disgrace, and frequent reproof of a friend leads to distance. Even right correction has a measure. The book of ren ends with a limit on being right.
chapters.question: Whom have you corrected too often?

chapters.reflection: Confucius gives his daughter in marriage to Gongye Chang, who had been in prison though not guilty, and his niece to Nan Rong, a man who would keep office in good times and avoid punishment in bad. The book records these as judgements of character. The chapter belongs to a world where a father or uncle arranged a marriage, and it reads as such.
chapters.question: What would you want to know about a person before trusting them with someone you love?

chapters.reflection: Confucius praises Zijian as a junzi, and then asks: if Lu had no junzi, where could he have acquired this? Character is learned from those around us. The praise of one person is also praise of a place.
chapters.question: From whom, around you, did you take the qualities you are proudest of?

chapters.reflection: Zigong asks what the Master thinks of him. "You are a vessel." Which kind? "A sacrificial vessel of jade." After II.12, that the junzi is not a vessel, the answer is both praise and limit: precious and fine, and still made for a purpose.
chapters.question: If someone you respect described you as a vessel, which kind would they name?

chapters.reflection: Someone remarks that Ran Yong is good but not eloquent. What use is a ready tongue, Confucius answers; quick retorts mostly earn dislike. Whether Yong is fully ren he does not know, but eloquence is beside the point.
chapters.question: Do you value quick speech in others more than it deserves?

chapters.reflection: Confucius urges Qidiao Kai to take office, and Kai replies that he does not yet trust himself in it. The Master is pleased. Knowing that one is not ready is itself a kind of readiness.
chapters.question: What are you not yet ready for, and how do you know?

chapters.reflection: My Way does not go forward, Confucius says; I will take a raft and float out to sea, and Zilu would come with me. Zilu is delighted. The Master adds that Zilu loves daring more than he does. Legge reads the last words as a lack of judgement; others read them as "there is nowhere to get the timber". Either way, a moment of discouragement turns into gentle teasing.
chapters.question: Who would follow you onto the raft, and would you want them to?

chapters.reflection: Meng Wu asks whether Zilu, Ran Qiu and Gongxi Chi are humane. Confucius describes each one's ability exactly, an army, a town, a court reception, and each time says he does not know if they are ren. Talent is easy to name; goodness he will not grant on demand.
chapters.question: Could you describe what someone is good at without being able to say whether they are good?

chapters.reflection: Confucius asks Zigong whether he or Hui is better. How could I compare, says Zigong: Hui hears one thing and knows ten, I hear one and know two. The Master agrees, and in the Chinese adds that neither of them, he included, is equal to Hui. Legge reads it as "I grant you"; many others read "you and I are not equal to him".
chapters.question: Whom do you admire without envy, and what makes that possible?

chapters.reflection: Zai Yu sleeps during the day, and Confucius says rotten wood cannot be carved, nor a dung wall plastered. Then a second remark: he used to hear people's words and trust their conduct; now he hears their words and watches their conduct. Zai Yu taught him this. The harshest rebuke in the book ends in a lesson the teacher learned.
chapters.question: Whose actions taught you to stop relying on their words?

chapters.reflection: Confucius has never seen a truly steadfast person. Someone names Shen Cheng. But Cheng has desires, the Master answers; how could he be unbending? Firmness, in this sense, is freedom from being pulled by wants.
chapters.question: What wants most easily bend your resolve?

chapters.reflection: Zigong says that what he does not want others to do to him, he does not want to do to them. Confucius: Ci, this is not yet within your reach. The rule is stated perfectly and the Master answers that stating it is not the same as living it. The thought returns in XII.2 and XV.23.
chapters.question: Which principle do you state easily that you have not yet reached?

chapters.reflection: Zigong says the Master's culture and conduct could be learned from him, but his words on human nature and the Way of Heaven could not be heard. Either he rarely spoke of them, or they could not be grasped by hearing. The chapter marks the edge of what the disciples received.
chapters.question: What did a teacher of yours teach by example that they never put into words?

chapters.reflection: When Zilu heard something he had not yet been able to put into practice, he was only afraid of hearing something else. The impatient disciple has here a virtue: he does not let learning outrun doing.
chapters.question: What have you learned recently that you have not yet put into practice?

chapters.reflection: Why was Kong Wenzi given the posthumous name Wen, "cultured"? Because he was quick and loved learning, and was not ashamed to ask those beneath him. The title honours a habit, not an achievement.
chapters.question: Whom below you in some ranking could you learn from, if you asked?

chapters.reflection: Zichan, the great minister of Zheng, had four marks of the junzi: humble in his own conduct, respectful to superiors, kind in caring for the people, just in employing them. The list looks in four directions, self, above, below, and the tasks given to others.
chapters.question: In which of the four directions are you weakest?

chapters.reflection: Yan Ping knew how to keep friendships: however long he knew someone, he showed them the same respect as at first. Familiarity did not wear the courtesy down.
chapters.question: With whom has long acquaintance worn away your first respect?

chapters.reflection: Zang Wenzhong kept a great divining tortoise in a house decorated with carved hills and painted water plants, ornaments fit for a ruler's temple. How can that be called wisdom? He was famed as wise, and Confucius notes where he was not.
chapters.question: What lavish habit undermines a reputation you otherwise deserve?

chapters.reflection: Zizhang asks about two officials: one who took and left office without joy or resentment and briefed his successor; one who abandoned his wealth rather than serve a regicide. Confucius calls the first loyal and the second pure, and of each says he does not know how they could be called ren. Fine single virtues do not add up to the whole.
chapters.question: Is there a single virtue you have that you mistake for the whole of goodness?

chapters.reflection: Ji Wenzi thought three times before acting. Confucius, hearing it, says twice will do. Reflection has a measure too: past a point it becomes hesitation.
chapters.question: What decision are you thinking over a third time?

chapters.reflection: When his state had the Way, Ning Wuzi was wise; when it lost the Way, he played the fool. His wisdom can be equalled, his foolishness cannot. In a dangerous court, appearing harmless can be the harder art.
chapters.question: When is it wiser to seem less clever than you are?

chapters.reflection: Travelling in Chen, Confucius exclaims: let me return! The young men of my school are ambitious and hasty, they have finished patterns but do not know how to cut them. He longs to shape them. A teacher abroad thinks of his students.
chapters.question: What work at home do you miss when you are away from it?

chapters.reflection: Bo Yi and Shu Qi, the two brothers who starved rather than serve a conqueror, did not keep old wrongs in mind, and so there was little resentment. Holding grudges keeps resentment alive on both sides.
chapters.question: What old wrong are you still keeping?

chapters.reflection: Who says Weisheng Gao is upright? Someone asked him for vinegar, and rather than say he had none, he begged some from a neighbour and handed it over as his own. A small vanity becomes a small dishonesty.
chapters.question: When have you pretended to have something you had to borrow?

chapters.reflection: Fine words, an ingratiating face, excessive deference: Zuo Qiuming was ashamed of them, and so is Confucius. Hiding resentment and befriending the person: the same. Shame here is a compass, pointing at insincerity.
chapters.question: Is there someone you treat as a friend while hiding resentment?

chapters.reflection: Confucius asks Yan Hui and Zilu for their wishes. Zilu would share his carriages and furs with friends without minding the wear. Hui would not boast of his goodness or display his merits. Asked in turn, the Master wishes rest for the old, good faith with friends, and tender care for the young.
chapters.question: If asked for your wishes in one sentence, what would you say?

chapters.reflection: It is hopeless, Confucius says; he has never seen anyone who could see his own faults and accuse himself inwardly. The chapter is a sigh. It also names the practice it says is missing.
chapters.question: When did you last see a fault of your own clearly, without excuse?

chapters.reflection: In a hamlet of ten households there must be someone as loyal and trustworthy as I am, Confucius says, but not one who loves learning as I do. He claims little for his virtue and much for his appetite to learn.
chapters.question: What do you love learning about, more than most people around you?

chapters.reflection: Confucius says Ran Yong could sit facing south, the position of a ruler. Yong then asks about Zisang Bozi, whom the Master calls easy-going. Yong distinguishes: being easy in small matters while serious within is acceptable; being easy within and easy in practice is too much. The Master agrees with him.
chapters.question: Where in your work is ease a strength, and where is it carelessness?

chapters.reflection: Duke Ai asks which disciple loved learning. Yan Hui did: he did not shift his anger onto others, and he did not make the same mistake twice. He died young, and there is no one like him now. Love of learning is described entirely as conduct.
chapters.question: When did you last take out on someone an anger that was about something else?

chapters.reflection: Ran Qiu asks grain for the mother of Gongxi Chi, who has gone on a mission, and gives far more than the Master named; Chi travels with fat horses and fine furs. The junzi helps those in need, not those already well off. Then Yuan Si, made steward, refuses his salary, and Confucius tells him to accept it and give it to his neighbours.
chapters.question: Do you give more easily where it is seen, or where it is needed?

chapters.reflection: Speaking of Ran Yong, whose father was of low standing, Confucius says: if the calf of a plough ox is red and well horned, even if people would not use it, would the spirits of the hills and rivers refuse it? Worth is not inherited and not cancelled by birth.
chapters.question: Where have you judged someone by where they came from?

chapters.reflection: Hui's heart did not depart from ren for three months together; the others reach it for a day or a month, and no more. The chapter treats goodness as something sustained over time, measured in months and days.
chapters.question: How long can you keep a good intention before it lapses?

chapters.reflection: Ji Kangzi asks whether Zilu, Zigong and Ran Qiu could hold office. Zilu is decisive, Zigong perceptive, Ran Qiu versatile: what difficulty would they have? Office, unlike ren, the Master grants readily.
chapters.question: What is your one strength that would make you fit for a task?

chapters.reflection: The Ji family asks Min Ziqian to govern Bi. Decline for me politely, he says, and if they ask again, I will be across the river Wen, out of the state. He refuses to serve a family that has usurped power, and he refuses with courtesy.
chapters.question: Have you ever refused an offer for a reason you kept to yourself?

chapters.reflection: Boniu is gravely ill. Confucius visits and holds his hand through the window. "It is fate. That such a man should have such an illness!" he says twice. The scene is one of the most personal in the book, grief without explanation.
chapters.question: How do you stay with someone when there is nothing to be done?

chapters.reflection: A basket of rice, a gourd of water, a mean lane: others could not bear the hardship, and Hui did not let it change his joy. Worthy indeed was Hui. The praise begins and ends with the same words, as if the Master could not say it once.
chapters.question: What joy of yours does not depend on comfort?

chapters.reflection: Ran Qiu says it is not that he does not love the Way, but his strength is not enough. Those whose strength fails collapse halfway, Confucius answers, but you are drawing a line in advance. The limit he describes is not exhaustion but a decision.
chapters.question: Where have you drawn a line before reaching it?
chapters.exercise: Take one thing you have decided you cannot do and do the first small part of it today.

chapters.reflection: Confucius tells Zixia to be a ru of the junzi kind, not of the small man's kind. Ru later became the name of the whole Confucian school; here it means a man of learning. The warning is that learning alone does not decide what kind of person one is.
chapters.question: What kind of learned person do you want to be?

chapters.reflection: Ziyou, governor of Wucheng, is asked if he has found good people. One, Tantai Mieming, never takes a short cut when walking and never comes to the governor's house except on public business. Two small habits, and they say everything about his integrity.
chapters.question: What small habit of yours would tell a stranger the most about you?

chapters.reflection: Meng Zhifan did not boast. Covering the retreat after a defeat, he whipped his horse as they reached the gate and said he had not dared to be last, his horse just would not go faster. He turns his courage into a joke about his horse.
chapters.question: How do you take credit, when you have earned it?

chapters.reflection: Without the glib tongue of Tuo the priest and the good looks of Song Zhao, Confucius says, it is hard to get by in this age. It is bitter. The two men were famous for winning favour with talk and with beauty.
chapters.question: What qualities does your own age reward that it should not?

chapters.reflection: Who can leave a house except by the door? Why then does no one go by this Way? The Way is as obvious as the door, and still people climb out of windows.
chapters.question: What obvious door are you avoiding?

chapters.reflection: When substance outweighs refinement, a person is rustic; when refinement outweighs substance, they are like a clerk. Only when the two are balanced is there a junzi. Neither raw honesty nor polish is enough alone.
chapters.question: Which do you have more of, substance or refinement?

chapters.reflection: People are born upright; one who lives without uprightness escapes by luck. Legge reads it as a claim about human nature, an early hint of the later debate about whether nature is good. It is also simply a warning.
chapters.question: Do you think people are born upright, or become so?

chapters.reflection: Knowing something is not as good as loving it; loving it is not as good as delighting in it. Three degrees of relation to the same thing, each closer than the last.
chapters.question: What do you know, what do you love, and what do you delight in?

chapters.reflection: To those above the middle one can speak of higher things; to those below, not. It sounds hierarchical and is mostly practical: teaching must meet the learner where they are. The book shows Confucius doing this again and again, giving different answers to the same question.
chapters.question: When have you explained something above or below the level of the person in front of you?

chapters.reflection: Fan Chi asks about wisdom: devote yourself to what is right for the people, respect the spirits and keep them at a distance. About ren: put the hard work first and the reward after. Both answers point toward the human and the present.
chapters.question: Do you more often think of the reward before the work, or after?

chapters.reflection: The wise delight in water, the humane in mountains; the wise are active, the humane still; the wise are joyful, the humane long-lived. The pairing is poetic, not a rule: two temperaments, each true in its way.
chapters.question: Are you more drawn to water or to mountains?

chapters.reflection: With one change Qi could reach the level of Lu; with one change Lu could reach the Way. Lu was the home of the Zhou rites, Qi the more powerful state. Confucius sees reform as close, just one step away in each case.
chapters.question: What one change would bring something you care about to where it should be?

chapters.reflection: A gu was a ritual drinking vessel, named for its corners. A gu that is not a gu: what a gu, what a gu! The things have changed and the names remain. It is the setting of names right, zhengming, without the word.
chapters.question: What word do you still use for something that no longer matches it?

chapters.reflection: Zai Wo tests the Master: if a humane person were told someone had fallen into a well, would he jump in after them? Why would he? The junzi can be made to go to the well, not to throw himself in; he can be deceived, not made a fool of. Goodness is not the same as stupidity.
chapters.question: When has someone used your goodness against your judgement?

chapters.reflection: The junzi studies widely in culture and draws it together with ritual, and so does not go astray. Breadth needs a binding, or it scatters.
chapters.question: What holds together everything you have learned?

chapters.reflection: Confucius visits Nanzi, the wife of the ruler of Wei, a woman with a scandalous name. Zilu is displeased, and the Master swears: if I have done wrong, may Heaven reject me. The book keeps a moment where the teacher must defend himself to his student.
chapters.question: When have you had to defend yourself to someone who expected better of you?

chapters.reflection: The virtue of the mean, zhongyong, is the highest, and it has long been rare among the people. The phrase gave its name to a whole book, the Doctrine of the Mean, which this app keeps in Lore.
chapters.question: Where in your life is the middle way the hardest to keep?

chapters.reflection: Zigong imagines someone who benefits all the people; would that be ren? It would be sagehood, beyond what even Yao and Shun achieved. The humane person, wishing to be established, helps others be established; wishing to succeed, helps others succeed. To take what is near in oneself as the measure for others: that is the method of ren.
chapters.question: What do you want for yourself that you could help someone else toward today?

chapters.reflection: Confucius describes himself as one who passes on rather than creates, trusting and loving the ancient ways, and compares himself to Old Peng, a figure from the distant past. It is a modest claim. The later tradition made him the founder of a school, which this chapter says he did not set out to be.
chapters.question: What do you pass on that you did not make?

chapters.reflection: To remember silently, to learn without tiring, to teach without wearying: which of these, Confucius asks, do I have? The question can be read as modesty or as a quiet claim to all three. VII.33 returns to the same two habits.
chapters.question: Which of the three comes most easily to you?

chapters.reflection: Virtue not cultivated, learning not discussed, hearing what is right and not moving toward it, not changing what is not good: these are the Master's worries. They are all failures of follow-through.
chapters.question: Which of the four is your own worry?

chapters.reflection: At home and at ease, the Master was relaxed and cheerful. The disciples recorded not only what he taught but how he looked when he was not teaching.
chapters.question: How do you look when no one needs anything from you?

chapters.reflection: How I have declined, Confucius says; for a long time I have not dreamed of the Duke of Zhou, the founder of the institutions he loved. Old age is felt as the loss of a dream.
chapters.question: Whom or what did you once dream of that you no longer do?

chapters.reflection: Set your will on the Way, base yourself on virtue, rely on ren, and take your ease in the arts. The four lines move from aim to footing to support to recreation. The arts here are ritual, music, archery, driving, writing and counting.
chapters.question: Where do you take your ease?

chapters.reflection: From anyone who brought even a small bundle of dried meat as a gift, the customary token for a teacher, Confucius never refused instruction. The door was open to any who came with the smallest sign of wanting to learn.
chapters.question: What small sign shows that you are ready to be taught?

chapters.reflection: Confucius does not open the way for someone who is not eager, nor prompt one who is not struggling to put it into words. If he shows one corner and the student cannot return with the other three, he does not repeat himself. Teaching requires effort from both sides.
chapters.question: When were you last shown one corner and found the other three yourself?

chapters.reflection: Eating beside someone in mourning, he never ate his fill; on a day he had wept, he did not sing. Two small observances of fellow feeling. Grief, even someone else's, changes what one does.
chapters.question: How do you change your conduct around someone who is grieving?

chapters.reflection: Confucius tells Yan Hui that only they two can take office when employed and withdraw when not. Zilu, wanting a share, asks whom the Master would take to lead an army. Not one who fights a tiger bare-handed or crosses a river without a boat and dies without regret, but one who goes into action with caution and a plan. Courage without care is not what he wants.
chapters.question: Where are you brave in a way that is only careless?

chapters.reflection: If wealth could be properly sought, Confucius says, he would do even the lowly job of holding a whip; if not, he follows what he loves. He is not against wealth, he is against pursuing it at any price.
chapters.question: What would you do for money, and what would you not?

chapters.reflection: The things he treated with the greatest care: fasting before sacrifice, war and illness. Each involves life and death, or the spirits, and none can be taken lightly.
chapters.question: What in your life deserves more care than you give it?

chapters.reflection: In Qi, Confucius heard the Shao music and for three months did not notice the taste of meat. He had not imagined music could reach such a height. The book records one experience of art so strong it displaced appetite.
chapters.question: What work of art has affected you so strongly that it changed your ordinary days?

chapters.reflection: The disciples wonder whether Confucius supports the ruler of Wei, who was fighting his own father for the throne. Zigong asks instead about Bo Yi and Shu Qi, two brothers who each gave up a throne to the other. They sought ren and got it; why would they complain? Zigong comes out and says the Master is not for the ruler.
chapters.question: When have you understood someone's answer to a question you did not ask directly?

chapters.reflection: Coarse rice to eat, water to drink, a bent arm for a pillow: there is joy in these too. Wealth and honour gained wrongly are to him like floating clouds. It is one of the book's best-known pictures of contentment.
chapters.question: What simple thing gives you joy?
chapters.exercise: Find one ordinary pleasure today, a drink of water or a quiet minute, and notice it fully.

chapters.reflection: Given more years, Confucius says, he would study the Yi, the Book of Changes, and might then be without great faults. The chapter is the main textual link between Confucius and the Changes. Some editions read a different character for Yi, and the line becomes "even so", without the book at all.
chapters.question: What would you study if you were given more years?

chapters.reflection: When he spoke of the Odes, the Documents and the observance of ritual, the Master used the standard pronunciation, the elegant speech of the court rather than his local dialect. Legge reads it as "his frequent themes". Either way, these were what he spoke of with care.
chapters.question: What subjects do you speak of with special care?

chapters.reflection: The Duke of She asks Zilu about Confucius, and Zilu does not answer. Why not tell him, says the Master, that I am someone who forgets to eat in my eagerness, forgets my worries in my joy, and does not notice old age coming? It is the most cheerful self-portrait in the book.
chapters.question: How would you want someone to describe you, if they had one sentence?

chapters.reflection: I was not born knowing, Confucius says; I love the ancients and seek it diligently. He claims effort, not a gift.
chapters.question: What do you know only because you worked to learn it?

chapters.reflection: The Master did not talk about prodigies, feats of strength, disorder or spirits. The list tells as much about him as any saying: his attention was on ordinary human conduct.
chapters.question: What subjects do you choose not to talk about?

chapters.reflection: Walking with two others, I am sure to find my teacher among them: I follow their good points and correct in myself their bad ones. Every companion is a lesson, either way.
chapters.question: What did the last two people you spent time with teach you?
chapters.exercise: With the next two people you meet today, find one quality to follow and one to avoid.

chapters.reflection: Huan Tui, a military officer of Song, tried to kill Confucius. Heaven gave me my virtue, the Master says; what can Huan Tui do to me? It is a moment of calm in danger, grounded in a sense of mission.
chapters.question: What gives you steadiness when you are threatened?

chapters.reflection: Do you think I hide anything from you? I hide nothing; there is nothing I do that I do not share with you. The teacher answers a suspicion that he holds back secret teachings. His whole life is the lesson.
chapters.question: Do the people close to you know how you actually live?

chapters.reflection: He taught four things: culture, conduct, loyalty and good faith. Legge renders them as letters, ethics, devotion of soul and truthfulness. Two are learned in books and two only in life.
chapters.question: Which of the four did your own education leave out?

chapters.reflection: A sage I shall not see; a junzi would be enough. A good person I shall not see; someone constant would be enough. But pretending to have when one has not, to be full when empty, at ease when pressed: it is hard for such people to be constant. Pretence is the enemy of steadiness.
chapters.question: Where are you pretending to more than you have?

chapters.reflection: The Master fished with a line but not with a net, and shot with an arrow but not at roosting birds. He took what he needed and left the rest a fair chance. Restraint applied even to sport.
chapters.question: Where could you take less than you are able to?

chapters.reflection: Some act without knowing; Confucius does not. He hears much, chooses the good and follows it, sees much and remembers it: this is the second kind of knowledge, below the knowledge one is born with. He places himself firmly in the second rank.
chapters.question: How much of what you know did you choose deliberately, from many sources?

chapters.reflection: The people of Huxiang were hard to talk to, and the disciples are surprised that Confucius receives a boy from there. He approves of his coming forward, not of what he may do after; why be so severe? If someone purifies himself to come, accept the purity without vouching for his past.
chapters.question: Whom do you refuse a fresh start because of where they come from?

chapters.reflection: Is ren far away? I wish for it, and here it is. After so many chapters where the Master refuses to call anyone ren, this one says it is as close as the wish. Both are true in the book: it is rare in a whole life and near in any moment.
chapters.question: What good act is within reach of you right now?

chapters.reflection: A minister of Chen asks whether Duke Zhao of Lu knew ritual, and Confucius says he did. Afterwards the minister points out that the duke married a woman of his own clan, against ritual, and disguised her name. Told of this, Confucius says: I am fortunate; if I make a mistake, people are sure to notice. He had defended his own ruler, and he accepts the correction gracefully.
chapters.question: How do you respond when someone points out your mistake?

chapters.reflection: When someone sang well in his company, the Master would ask them to sing again and then join in. A small detail of pleasure in another's gift, and of joining rather than judging.
chapters.question: Whose talent could you join in with, rather than only admire?

chapters.reflection: In learning I may be as good as others, Confucius says, but in practising what the junzi practises, I have not yet succeeded. He separates scholarship from conduct and grades himself low on the second.
chapters.question: Which do you rate yourself higher in, knowing or doing?

chapters.reflection: How could I dare call myself a sage or ren? It may be said only that I strive without tiring and teach without weariness. Gongxi Chi answers that this is exactly what the disciples cannot learn from him. The modest claim turns out to be the hardest.
chapters.question: What do you do without tiring that others find hard?

chapters.reflection: When the Master is gravely ill, Zilu asks to pray for him, citing a text of prayers to the spirits above and below. Is there such a thing? Confucius asks, and then says: my praying has been going on a long time. It may mean his whole life has been a prayer, or that he does not need Zilu's. The chapter keeps the ambiguity.
chapters.question: What in your daily life could be called a kind of prayer?

chapters.reflection: Extravagance leads to arrogance, frugality to shabbiness; better shabby than arrogant. Of two faults, he prefers the one that harms others less.
chapters.question: If you must err, which way do you err?

chapters.reflection: The junzi is calm and at ease; the small man is always anxious. The contrast is about inner weather, not outward fortune.
chapters.question: What made you anxious today, and was it within your control?

chapters.reflection: The Master was gentle yet stern, commanding yet not harsh, respectful yet at ease. Each quality is held with its opposite. Book VII ends with a portrait, not a saying.
chapters.question: Which pair of qualities would you most like to hold together?

chapters.reflection: Taibo, eldest son of an early Zhou lord, three times gave up his claim to the throne so that a younger line could rule, and did it so quietly that the people had nothing to praise. Confucius calls this the highest virtue. Goodness that leaves no mark to applaud is put at the top.
chapters.question: What good could you do today that no one would know to thank you for?

chapters.reflection: Respect without ritual becomes tiresome, caution becomes timidity, courage becomes disorder, frankness becomes rudeness. Each good quality needs a form to hold it in shape. The second half adds that when those above are devoted to their families and do not forget old friends, the people follow.
chapters.question: Which of your good qualities turns into a fault when it has no form?

chapters.reflection: Dying, Master Zeng asks his students to uncover his hands and feet: his body, received from his parents, is whole. He quotes the Odes on walking as if on the edge of an abyss, as if on thin ice, and says that from now on he knows he is free of that care. Keeping the body unharmed was, for him, part of filial piety.
chapters.question: What have you been carrying carefully all your life, and why?

chapters.reflection: When a bird is about to die its cry is sad; when a man is about to die his words are good. Master Zeng then tells the visiting noble three things that matter: bearing without violence, a face close to sincerity, speech without coarseness. The ritual vessels, he adds, have their own officers. He sends the great man back to his own conduct.
chapters.question: If you had only three things to tell someone in power, what would they be?

chapters.reflection: Able, yet asking those less able; rich in knowledge, yet asking those who have little; having, as if not having; full, as if empty; wronged, and not disputing it: Master Zeng once had a friend like this. Tradition takes the friend to be Yan Hui.
chapters.question: Which of these five do you find hardest?

chapters.reflection: Someone who can be entrusted with a young orphan prince and the government of a state, and who cannot be moved in a great crisis: is this a junzi? Yes, a junzi. Master Zeng defines the junzi by trustworthiness under pressure.
chapters.question: What would you trust to someone only if you were sure they could not be moved?

chapters.reflection: The scholar must be broad and resolute, for the load is heavy and the road long. Ren is the load: is that not heavy? Only death ends the road: is that not long? Master Zeng's picture of the moral life has no finish line before the last.
chapters.question: What load have you taken on that will last as long as you do?

chapters.reflection: One is roused by the Odes, established by ritual, and completed by music. Three arts and three stages: feeling, form, harmony. Education here is aesthetic as much as moral.
chapters.question: Which art first roused you?

chapters.reflection: The people can be made to follow, not made to understand. The chapter is often read as contempt for ordinary people, and it can be. It can also be read as a statement of fact about government: example moves people further than explanation. A different punctuation of the Chinese, proposed by some scholars, makes it say: let them follow if they can, and if not, teach them.
chapters.question: Have you ever followed someone well without understanding why?

chapters.reflection: A bold man who hates poverty will make trouble; so will a man without ren if he is hated too much. The second clause is the surprising one: excessive dislike of the bad can itself breed disorder.
chapters.question: Whom do you dislike so much that it might make things worse?

chapters.reflection: Even with the talents of the Duke of Zhou, if a person is proud and stingy, the rest is not worth looking at. The Duke was Confucius's model statesman. Talent cannot redeem arrogance and meanness.
chapters.question: What talent of yours might be cancelled by a habit you do not see?

chapters.reflection: It is hard to find someone who has studied three years without thinking of a salary. Legge reads the end differently, as "without coming to be good". The usual modern reading is the salary one, which fits II.18.
chapters.question: When did you last learn something without thinking of what it would earn you?

chapters.reflection: Hold firmly to good faith and love learning; keep to the good Way until death. Do not enter a state in danger or stay in one in disorder; show yourself when the world has the Way and hide when it does not. When the state has the Way, to be poor is shameful; when it lacks the Way, to be rich is shameful.
chapters.question: In the world as it is now, what kind of success would be shameful?

chapters.reflection: One who does not hold the office does not plan its policy. The sentence is plain about responsibility: authority and the right to decide come together. It returns in XIV.26.
chapters.question: Where are you deciding things that are not your responsibility?

chapters.reflection: When the music master Zhi began, the finale of the Guanju flooded the ears. A memory of a performance, recorded with pleasure. The book has room for a concert remembered.
chapters.question: What performance do you still remember in your ears?

chapters.reflection: Ardent but not upright, ignorant but not careful, simple but not honest: such people Confucius does not understand. Each pair joins a weakness to the absence of the virtue that usually comes with it.
chapters.question: What combination in people puzzles you most?

chapters.reflection: Study as if you cannot catch up, and still fear losing what you have. The urgency of learning in two directions: forward, and holding on.
chapters.question: What are you afraid of losing that you once learned?

chapters.reflection: How sublime Shun and Yu were: they held the whole world and it was as if it were nothing to them. Possession without attachment is the mark of the sage kings.
chapters.question: What do you possess that you could hold more lightly?

chapters.reflection: Only Heaven is great, and only Yao modelled himself on it. His virtue was so vast the people had no name for it; his achievements and his culture shone. The chapter praises the first of the sage kings in the language of awe.
chapters.question: Whom do you admire so much that words for it run out?

chapters.reflection: Shun had five ministers; King Wu said he had ten. Confucius notes how rare talent is, adding, in Legge's reading, that one of the ten was a woman, so the able ministers were only nine men. The chapter's point is the rarity of talent; the way it counts shows the assumption of its world, that office belonged to men, while still naming the woman among the ten. It ends by praising the Zhou for still serving the Shang when they held two thirds of the realm.
chapters.question: Whose talent around you goes uncounted because of who they are?

chapters.reflection: Yu the Great, who tamed the floods, ate simply but was generous to the spirits, dressed plainly but wore fine robes at sacrifice, lived in a low house but spent his strength on the irrigation channels. Confucius can find no fault. Private frugality, public generosity.
chapters.question: Where do you spend on yourself what should go to the common good?

chapters.reflection: The Master rarely spoke of profit, of fate and of ren. The last item is puzzling, since ren is everywhere in the book. One reading is that he rarely spoke of it in the abstract, only in answers to particular people; another reading of the grammar makes him rarely speak of profit, but approve of fate and ren.
chapters.question: What do you value most that you rarely speak of directly?

chapters.reflection: A villager says Confucius is great, broadly learned, but famous for nothing in particular. The Master jokes: what should I specialise in? Archery? Driving? I will take up driving. Driving was the humblest of the gentlemanly arts. He answers praise mixed with criticism with self-mockery.
chapters.question: How do you answer praise that carries a hidden criticism?

chapters.reflection: The ritual cap should be of linen; now silk is used because it is cheaper, and Confucius follows the majority. Ritual requires bowing below the hall; now people bow only after ascending, which is presumptuous, and he keeps the old way against the majority. He changes where change is harmless and resists where it shows disrespect.
chapters.question: Which customs have you let change, and which do you keep against the crowd?

chapters.reflection: He had no fixed preconceptions, no insistence on certainty, no stubbornness, no self-centredness. Four absences describe the Master as well as any list of virtues.
chapters.question: Which of the four do you most need to be free of?

chapters.reflection: Surrounded and threatened in Kuang, where he was mistaken for a man who had wronged the town, Confucius says: King Wen is dead, but is culture not here with me? If Heaven meant culture to perish, it would not have given it to me; if not, what can the people of Kuang do? Like VII.22, a moment of composure resting on a sense of what he carried.
chapters.question: What are you carrying that matters more than your own safety?

chapters.reflection: An official asks Zigong whether the Master is a sage, he has so many skills. Zigong says Heaven made him nearly a sage and gave him many abilities. Confucius corrects them: he was poor when young, so he learned many humble skills. Does the junzi need many? Not many. He refuses to have his practical skills counted as wisdom.
chapters.question: What skill did you learn only because you had to?

chapters.reflection: Do I have knowledge? No. But if a simple man asks me something, even if I am empty, I take up the question from both ends and exhaust it. His method is not a store of answers but a way of examining questions.
chapters.question: What question are you facing that you have only looked at from one end?

chapters.reflection: The phoenix does not come, the river gives no chart: it is over for me. Both were omens of a sage ruler's appearance. Confucius despairs of living to see good government. It is a rare moment of personal hopelessness.
chapters.question: What sign are you waiting for that has not come?

chapters.reflection: When he saw someone in mourning, someone in official dress, or a blind person, he would rise even if they were young, and pass them with hurried steps. Respect is shown in the body.
chapters.question: How does your body show respect, without words?

chapters.reflection: Yan Hui sighs: the more I look up, the higher it is; the more I bore into it, the harder; I see it before me and suddenly it is behind. The Master leads step by step, broadens me with culture and restrains me with ritual. I cannot stop, and when I have used all my strength, something stands sheer before me, and I find no way to follow. It is the most moving account of a student's experience in the book.
chapters.question: What have you pursued that always seemed to stay just ahead?

chapters.reflection: When the Master was very ill, Zilu had disciples act as his retainers, as if he still held office. Recovering, Confucius rebukes him: whom would I deceive? Heaven? Better to die in the arms of you, my disciples, than among retainers. Even if I have no grand burial, will I die by the roadside? He wants the truth of his situation honoured, not a fiction.
chapters.question: Where have you kept up an appearance that deceives no one?

chapters.reflection: Zigong asks: if there were a beautiful jade, should one hide it in a box or sell it for a good price? Sell it, sell it, Confucius says; I am waiting for a buyer. The jade is the Master himself, waiting for a ruler who would employ him.
chapters.question: What gift of yours are you keeping in a box?

chapters.reflection: Confucius wants to go and live among the eastern tribes. Someone objects that they are uncouth. If a junzi lived among them, what uncouthness would there be? The answer combines the cultural confidence of his time with a belief that conduct transforms a place.
chapters.question: What place would you change by living in it well?

chapters.reflection: After returning from Wei to Lu, Confucius put the music in order, and the court songs and hymns each found their proper place. It is one of the few concrete achievements the book credits to him.
chapters.question: What have you put back in order that had drifted?

chapters.reflection: To serve high officials abroad and father and elder brothers at home, to give all one can to funerals, and not to be troubled by wine: what difficulty do I have with these? Legge reads the end as "which of these do I attain to?", a modest question. Others read it as a quiet claim that these are within his reach.
chapters.question: What ordinary duties are you sure you manage, and are you right?

chapters.reflection: Standing by a river, the Master says: it passes on like this, never ceasing, day and night. The line has been read as grief at time passing and as praise of steady effort. Both readings are old.
chapters.question: What, in your life, keeps passing on like the river?
chapters.exercise: Stand for a minute by moving water, or watch rain, and think of one thing that has been flowing through your days.

chapters.reflection: I have never seen anyone who loves virtue as much as they love beauty. The sentence repeats in XV.13. The comparison is with an attraction that needs no effort at all.
chapters.question: What good do you love as easily as a beautiful face?

chapters.reflection: Learning is like raising a mound: if one basket short I stop, it is I who stop. It is like levelling ground: if I add one basket, it is I who advance. Progress and failure are both one's own, one basket at a time.
chapters.question: What one basket of earth would you add today?
chapters.exercise: Do one small piece of a task you have stopped, just one basket's worth.

chapters.reflection: The one who never grew tired when I spoke to him: that was Hui. A short memory of a student's attention.
chapters.question: When do you listen without growing tired?

chapters.reflection: Of Yan Hui, after his death: alas, I saw him advance, I never saw him stop. Grief and praise in one breath.
chapters.question: What would you want said of you, that someone saw you advance?

chapters.reflection: There are sprouts that never flower and flowers that never fruit. The image is often taken as a lament for Yan Hui, dead before his promise was fulfilled. It speaks of any promise that does not ripen.
